choices: By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train has already left and the ticket office had closed for the night.
By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train had already left and the ticket office has closed for the night.
By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train has already left and the ticket office has closed for the night.
By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train had already left and the ticket office had closed for the night.
correct_answer: By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train had already left and the ticket office had closed for the night.
error_sites: 'had already left' (past perfect) for the first action finished before Grandpa arrived
'had closed' (past perfect) for the second action finished before Grandpa arrived

student_error.By the time Grandpa arrived at the stati: Uses present perfect 'has left' for an action that was finished before another past action.
Gets the first verb right but slips into present perfect 'has closed' for the second earlier action.
Uses present perfect 'has' for both earlier actions, not knowing that a past event needs 'had'.

explanation: The sentence is set in the past (arrived). Both the train leaving and the office closing happened before Grandpa arrived, so both need the past perfect: 'had already left' and 'had closed'. Present perfect 'has' does not fit an action completed before another past action.
varied_dimension: past perfect vs present perfect, first verb; past perfect vs present perfect, second verb

Neither the twins or their older brother knows how to fix the bike chain, so they asked a neighbor for help.
correct_answer: Neither the twins nor their older brother knows how to fix the bike chain, so they asked a neighbor for help.

student_error.Neither the twins nor their older brothe: Makes the verb plural because 'the twins' come first, instead of agreeing with the nearer subject 'brother'.
student_error.Neither the twins or their older brother: Does not know how correlative conjunctions work, either in the pairing or in agreement.

explanation: 'Neither' is always paired with 'nor'. With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'their older brother', so it is singular: 'knows'.
varied_dimension: correlative pair (neither/nor); verb agreement with the nearer subject

error_sites: 'me' as part of the object of 'asked'
'she and I' as the subject of 'carried'

student_error.Coach Diaz asked Priya and I to collect: Uses 'I' after 'and' because 'Priya and I' sounds more correct, though the pronoun is an object.
student_error.Coach Diaz asked Priya and me to collect: Uses the object forms 'her and me' as the subject of 'carried'.
student_error.Coach Diaz asked Priya and I to collect: Chooses pronoun case by sound instead of by its job in the sentence.

explanation: 'me' is the object of 'asked' (Coach asked me). 'she and I' is the subject of 'carried' (she carried, I carried), so it uses subject pronouns.
varied_dimension: objective case in a compound object; subjective case in a compound subject

student_error.Jamal and myself painted the whole fence: Uses 'myself' as a subject because it sounds more formal.
student_error.Jamal and I painted the whole fence by o: Uses the nonstandard form 'hisself' for the intensive pronoun.
student_error.Jamal and myself painted the whole fence: Does not know the standard uses and forms of -self pronouns.

choices: Running for the bus, his lunch fell out of his bag, so sitting in math class, his stomach growled nonstop.
While Theo was running for the bus, his lunch fell out of his bag, so during math class, his stomach growled nonstop.
While Theo was running for the bus, his lunch fell out of his bag, so sitting in math class, his stomach growled nonstop.
Running for the bus, his lunch fell out of his bag, so during math class, his stomach growled nonstop.
correct_answer: While Theo was running for the bus, his lunch fell out of his bag, so during math class, his stomach growled nonstop.
error_sites: the opening modifier with its own subject 'Theo'

student_error.Running for the bus, his lunch fell out: Starts with 'Running for the bus', which then describes 'his lunch' instead of Theo.
student_error.While Theo was running for the bus, his: Uses 'sitting in math class', which then describes 'his stomach' instead of Theo.
student_error.Running for the bus, his lunch fell out: Does not check what the -ing phrase attaches to, because the meaning seems clear.

explanation: An -ing phrase describes the subject that comes right after it. 'Running for the bus' would describe 'his lunch' and 'sitting in math class' would describe 'his stomach'. Giving the first clause its own subject (While Theo was running) and using 'during' avoids both dangling modifiers.
varied_dimension: dangling opening participial phrase; dangling participial phrase after a conjunction

error_sites: no repeated 'she' after the clause 'who drives it every day'

student_error.Although the bus was late, but Ms. Chu,: Adds 'but' after an 'although' clause, using two connecting words for one link.
student_error.Although the bus was late, Ms. Chu, who: Repeats the subject as 'she' because the 'who' clause separates 'Ms. Chu' from the verb.
student_error.Although the bus was late, but Ms. Chu,: Loses track of the sentence structure and adds extra connecting words and subjects.

explanation: 'Although' already links the two ideas, so 'but' is not used too. The subject 'Ms. Chu' goes with the verb 'got' even though a 'who' clause comes between them, so 'she' is not repeated.
varied_dimension: extra conjunction after a subordinate clause (although...but); repeated subject pronoun after an interrupting clause

student_error.The box of photos that my grandparents k: Makes the verb agree with the nearby plural 'photos' or 'grandparents' instead of the subject 'box'.
Makes the verb agree with 'pictures' instead of the subject 'each'.

student_error.When Ms. Ortiz asked for quiet, the clas: Uses 'stopped to talk', which means they stopped in order to talk, the opposite of the meaning needed.
Uses 'forgotten turning off', which means he forgot that he had done it, though the phone then rang.
Treats the gerund and infinitive after 'stop' and 'forget' as if they meant the same thing.

varied_dimension: gerund vs infinitive after 'stop'; infinitive vs gerund after 'forget'

student_error.If Omar had checked the weather before t: Uses 'would pack' for a result that would have happened last Saturday.
student_error.If Omar would have checked the weather b: Does not know the form of a condition about the past.

student_error.Before the test begins, sharpen your pen: Changes the second instruction into a statement ('you should write') after beginning with a command.
